chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, who said:

Two men came to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) regarding management and dealings between them. When he heard their speech, he said: 'Know that no one has achieved success with goodness from success achieved by injustice. Know that the oppressed one takes from the religion of the oppressor more than what the oppressor takes from the wealth of the oppressed one.'

Then he said: 'Whoever does evil to people should not deny evil when it is done to him. Know that indeed, the son of Adam reaps only what he sows, and no one harvests sweetness from bitterness, nor bitterness from sweetness.' So the two men reconciled before they stood up.
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence of injustice according to Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) resolves a dispute by highlighting the spiritual economy of justice, where the oppressed's patience and merit (*din*) outweigh the oppressor's material gain. He employs the agricultural metaphor of 'reaping what you sow' to illustrate that evil actions yield bitter consequences, a concept deeply rooted in Shia ethical teachings on *Adl* (justice) and *Hasanat* (merits). This practical wisdom not only facilitated immediate reconciliation but also underscores the theological principle that divine retribution is precise and proportional to one's deeds.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Al Hassan Bin Mahboub, from Ali Bin Abu Hamza, from Abu Baseer who said,

‘Two men came over to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> regarding management issues and dealings between the two of them. So when he<sup>asws</sup> heard both their speeches, said: ‘But no one would achieve success with goodness from a success achieved by the injustice. But, the oppressed one takes from the Religion of the unjust one more than what the unjust one takes from the wealth of the oppressed one’.

Then he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The one who does evil with the people should not deny the evil when it is done with him. But he, the son of Adam<sup>as</sup>, rather tends to reap what he sows, and no one has harvested sweetness from the bitterness, nor a bitterness from the sweetness’. So the two men reconciled before they arose’.
en.sarwar: 22. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Isa from al-Hassan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn abu Hamza from abu Basir who has said the following:

“Once two people came to see abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) about the differences that they had over a deal between them and when the Imam heard their case, he said, ‘To achieve victory through injustice is not victory in anything good. What the oppressed takes away from the religion of the oppressor is much more than what the oppressor takes from the property of the oppressed.’

The Imam then said, ‘Whoever does evil to people should call it evil when it is done to him. Is it not the case that children of Adam reap what they sow? No one expects to harvest sweet from sour and vice versa. The two men then agreed to a settlement before standing up to leave.’”
